newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia row hits Singapore shares, dealers say.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia row hits Singapore shares, dealers say.

text.p: Singapore's stock market lost more than one percent on Thursday in reaction to a bitter row between the island republic and Malaysia, one of its largest trading partners.

The main index fell 21 points in early trade but some market analysts said disappointing economic figures announced late on Wednesday were a more important factor, and questioned the long-term impact of the diplomatic flap.
"The market is taking its cue from the row with Malaysia over SM (Senior Minister) Lee's comments," a dealer with a Singapore brokerage, who declined to be identified, told Reuters.

On Wednesday, Malaysian newspapers reported Lee Kuan Yew's description of Malaysia's Johor state as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings" in an affidavit filed in a Singapore court on January 27 in relation to libel action against an opposition politician.

Malaysia asked for a retraction and apology over Lee's comments, and the news was a factor as Singapore's benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index (STII) fell 21.48 points to 2,155.91 by 0250 GMT on Thursday, dealers said.
At midday, the market was 16.64 points down from Wednesday at 2,160.75.
Dealers said investors were concerned that Singapore firms might be hit by economic retaliation, recalling a diplomatic row between Malaysia and Britain in 1995.
British firms were banned from tendering for Malaysian infrastructure contracts after a row erupted over a dam construction project.
"If he (Lee) doesn't backtrack, it's going to cost us a lot," said another dealer, who also declined to be identified.
But market analysts said poor industrial output figures released on Wednesday evening, showing a drop of 7.2 percent in manufacturing output year on year in January, were the real depressant.
"The industrial figures were worse than expected and show that the recovery is not here yet," said Violet Soh, analyst with Fraser Securities.

"Malaysia and Singapore are always falling out with each other, there's nothing new there. At the end of the day, both countries recognise they have a need for strong links with each other economically," said another analyst who asked not to be identified.
Singapore had not issued an official comment on the Malaysian request as of midday on Thursday, although a Ministry of Foreign Affairs statement was expected to come later in the day.
